source_refs.note: Topic 23.3.1 with Figure 23.2 and the side notes on Perspex and [H], printed pages 101-103 (PDF 104-106).

blocks.text: Aldehydes and ketones react with hydrogen cyanide to form cyanohydrins. HCN itself is not used directly as it is an extremely poisonous gas. Instead, it is produced by adding slowly a mineral acid (HCl) to a mixture of aqueous solution of sodium cyanide or potassium cyanide and the carbonyl compound.
2-Hydroxy-2-ethylpropanenitrile is used as an intermediate in the manufacture of Perspex, a very fine coloured-glass polymer.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The Perspex intermediate is the product of propanone and HCN drawn below, (CH₃)₂C(OH)CN: 2-hydroxy-2-methylpropanenitrile, not '2-ethyl'.

blocks.alt: Ethanal (H3C and H on a C double-bonded to O; C +delta, O -delta) + H-CN (H +delta, CN -delta), KCN/HCl over the arrow, gives 2-hydroxypropanenitrile: a C carrying H3C, OH, H and CN.
blocks.caption: Ethanal and HCN give 2-hydroxypropanenitrile (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure on PDF page 104).

blocks.alt: Propanone (two H3C groups on a C double-bonded to O; C +delta, O -delta) + H-CN, KCN/HCl over the arrow, gives 2-hydroxy-2-methylpropanenitrile: a C carrying two H3C groups, OH and CN.
blocks.caption: Propanone and HCN give 2-hydroxy-2-methylpropanenitrile (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure on PDF page 105).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The product name is printed '2-hydroxy-2-methlypropanenitrile'; it is spelt 2-hydroxy-2-methylpropanenitrile.

HCN is obtained by adding a controlled amount of an acid to a mixture of KCN and the carbonyl compound. The reaction between KCN and HCl produces HCN. HCN is neither a nucleophile (absence of a lone pair on the carbon atom) nor a strong acid to be ionized to a reasonable extent. Therefore it does not produce enough nucleophile (CN⁻) to start a reaction and complete the reaction in a shorter time. This is done by adding a slight excess of KCN, so that there are some free CN⁻ ions in the solution. These free ions start the reaction and catalyse it to move at a reasonable rate.

blocks.alt: Three steps. i) KCN (Excess) + HCl (Limiting) -> HCN (Nucleophilic Reagent) + KCl. ii) RHC=O (C +delta, O -delta) + cyanide ion, :C-triple bond-N with a negative charge, in equilibrium with the anion R, H, O- and C-triple bond-N on one carbon. iii) That anion + H-CN (H +delta, CN -delta) in equilibrium with the hydroxyalkanenitrile (OH in place of O-) + cyanide ion.
blocks.caption: Mechanism of the addition of HCN (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure on PDF page 105).

blocks.text: Although both the steps involved in cyanohydrin formation are reversible, the equilibria lie far to the right. Most of carbonyl compounds giving high yields of cyanohydrins at the equilibrium. Nitriles are hydrolysed by dilute acid or aqueous alkali to form carboxylic acids or carboxylate ions; this will be discussed later.

Since aldehydes and ketones are synthesised by oxidation of alcohols, alcohols can be produced by the reduction of aldehydes and ketones. With a reducing agent such as NaBH₄ or LiAlH₄, aldehydes give primary alcohols and ketones gives secondary alcohols.
Notice that reducing H in brackets [ ] comes from NaBH₄ to balance the equation. It does not represent atomic hydrogen.

blocks.alt: Two equations. Ethanal, CH3-C(=O)-H, + 2[H], with NaBH4 and delta (heat) over the arrow and H2O/OH- under it, gives ethanol, CH3-CH2-OH. Propanone, CH3-C(=O)-CH3, + 2[H], with NaBH4 Heat over the arrow and alkaline aqueous solution under it, gives propan-2-ol, CH3-CH(OH)-CH3.
blocks.caption: Reduction of ethanal and propanone with NaBH4 (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure on PDF page 105).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The propanone equation prints 'alkalineaqucoussolution' under the arrow and names the product 'propane-2-ol'; they are 'alkaline aqueous solution' and propan-2-ol.

blocks.alt: The hydride ion H:- (nucleophile) attacks the carbon of RHC=O (C +delta, O -delta; carbonyl compound): one curly arrow goes from the hydride's lone pair to C, another from the C=O bond to O. This gives the alkoxide ion R-CH2-O-. With H-OH (H +delta, OH -delta) over the next arrow, it gives the alcohol R-CH2-OH + :OH-.
blocks.caption: Mechanism of the reduction of a carbonyl compound by a hydride ion (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure on PDF page 106).

blocks.text: Aldehydes or ketones undergo a condensation reaction with 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazine (2,4-NDPH) to give an orange crystalline solids with well-defined melting points.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The abbreviation of 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazine is 2,4-DNPH (here and in the next paragraph), not 2,4-NDPH.

blocks.alt: Ethanal (H3C and H on C=O) + H2N-NH- attached to a benzene ring with NO2 opposite and O2N next to it (2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazine) -> ethanal-2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazone, in which the C=O has become C=N-NH- on the same ring, + H2O. Drawn as two rows: reactants, then products.
blocks.caption: Ethanal and 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazine give ethanal-2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazone and water (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure on PDF page 106).

blocks.text: This reagent is used to identify carbonyl compounds. For example, ethanal reacts with 2,4-NDPH to form orange crystals of 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazone. Other classes of organic compounds like carboxylic acids, esters, acyl halides, amides etc which also contain the carbonyl group >C=O do not give this test.

blocks.alt: Two test tubes: one of yellow-orange liquid, and one packed with orange crystals.
blocks.caption: Figure 23.2: Ethanal gives orange crystalline 2,4-DNPH (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 23.2).
